key_insight: The paper reframes update scheduling as a timing bandit problem and shows that exploiting consecutive feedback can nearly eliminate the extra factor of K in regret.
engineering_relevance: It offers a principled way to decide when to refresh costly systems like ML models or digital twins, balancing update overhead against performance drift.
method: Define each candidate update interval as an arm with fixed update cost plus stochastic degradation cost.
Use Balanced Consecutive Arm Elimination (BCAE) to leverage intermediate feedback from longer intervals and eliminate poor intervals efficiently.
Add an Optimism-Enhanced variant (OE-BCAE) with lower-confidence-bound exploration for better practical adaptivity.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports ~O(\sqrt{T}) regret for the proposed methods, matching the lower bound up to logarithmic factors, with simulations showing low regret and stability across varying arm counts and update costs.
watch_item: Performance depends on the validity of the assumed degradation and feedback structure, so real systems with nonstationary or delayed observations may require careful adaptation.
paper_title: Learning When to Update: A Near-Optimal Timing Bandit Approach
